notes.meaning: Joseph arrived in Egypt as a bought slave with no say in where he was taken. He was purchased by Potiphar, an Egyptian officer who commanded Pharaoh's royal bodyguards. Even in this hard place, God positioned Joseph inside the home of a high official where he could learn how government and leadership worked.

Even though Joseph was torn away from his family, he was never separated from God. The Lord stayed close to him, enabling him to do every task well and with great success. True success does not depend on having an easy life, but on having the Lord by our side.

Potiphar soon realized that Joseph was not an ordinary worker. The Egyptian master could see that everything Joseph handled turned out well because the true God was helping him. Joseph's steady honesty and skill showed an unbelieving master that the Lord was real.

Potiphar was so pleased with Joseph that he made him his personal attendant and head steward over his entire estate. Joseph managed all the servants, supplies, and daily business. Because he proved faithful with small tasks, his master trusted him with everything he owned.

As soon as Joseph took charge of the estate, the Lord poured out blessings on Potiphar's family, house, and fields. The Egyptian officer enjoyed peace and wealth simply because Joseph was serving him. This began to fulfill God's promise that other nations would be blessed through Abraham's family.

Potiphar trusted Joseph so completely that he never worried about money or property, only caring about the food on his table. During these years, Joseph grew into a handsome, strong young man, looking much like his mother Rachel. While his good looks were a blessing, they soon became the doorway to a severe trial.

After Joseph became powerful and successful in the household, Potiphar's wife began looking at him with lust. Egyptian women had a great deal of freedom in the home, and she bluntly told him to sleep with her. Joseph's season of honor brought an immediate and dangerous temptation.

Joseph flatly refused her and reminded her of the deep trust Potiphar had placed in him. His master had held nothing back except his own wife, so sleeping with her would be a terrible act of betrayal. Most of all, Joseph recognized that giving in would be a great wickedness and a direct sin against God.

Potiphar's wife did not give up, but repeated her improper offer day after day. Joseph remained steady and refused to listen, refusing even to stay in the same room with her. He knew that the safest way to avoid falling into sin is to stay far out of its path.

One day, Joseph went inside the house to carry out his regular work duties. None of the household servants happened to be inside the building at that time. This gave his master's wife a quiet, private setting to corner him once more.

She grabbed hold of Joseph's outer robe and demanded again that he sleep with her. Rather than staying to argue or put himself in danger, Joseph slipped out of his garment and ran outside. He chose to lose his coat rather than lose his purity.

When the woman saw that Joseph had fled and left his cloak in her hands, her desire quickly turned into bitter anger. She realized that her sinful plan had failed and that she held physical evidence of his escape. To protect her own pride and safety, she decided to twist the story and blame Joseph.

She called out to the household servants and claimed that the Hebrew slave had tried to force himself on her. She appealed to their prejudice against foreigners and claimed she screamed as loud as she could. Then she falsely insisted that Joseph dropped his cloak and ran away only because he heard her cries.

She kept Joseph's garment beside her to use as fake proof of her story. This was the second time in Joseph's life that a piece of clothing was used to tell a lie about him. She waited patiently until her husband returned from his duties to present her false evidence.

When Potiphar arrived home, she repeated the exact same dishonest story to him. She blamed her husband for bringing a Hebrew slave into their house to insult and mock her. She claimed once more that the young man fled and dropped his cloak only after she shouted for help.

Potiphar listened to his wife's report and flared up with intense anger. Because the story sounded convincing and she had the cloak, he accepted her words without examining the truth. The master who had trusted Joseph with everything now saw him as an ungrateful traitor.

Potiphar had Joseph arrested and thrown into the royal prison where the king's prisoners were kept. In Egyptian society, a slave accused of such a crime could easily have been executed on the spot. Even in this unfair suffering, God kept Joseph alive and placed him where the Lord's next plan would unfold.

Prison walls and iron chains could not shut out God's loving presence from Joseph. The Lord stayed close to him in the dungeon, showed him faithful kindness, and gave him favor with the head warden. Even when life seems at its lowest point, God never abandons His faithful people.

The warden soon trusted Joseph completely and put him in charge of all the other prisoners and daily prison operations. Just as in Potiphar's house, the warden did not need to watch over anything in Joseph's hands. Joseph prospered in everything he did because the Lord was with him and guided his steps.
